text:
WITH NEARLY DUE NORTH FLOW 
ALOFT BECOMING THE PREDOMINANT REGIME THE BALANCE OF THIS WEEK AND 
NEXT...ONLY ONE WAY TO GO WITH TEMPS AND THAT IS DOWN.

THESE SNOW SHOWERS WILL START IN THE LATE MORNING IN THE NW AND MOVE 
SOUTHEAST DURING THE AFTN...WITH THE DES MOINES METRO AREA GETTING 
THE SHOWERS OF FLUFF OFF AND ON BETWEEN NOON AND 5 PM.

MOISTURE CURRENTLY ADVECTING FROM 
NEBRASKA INTO WEST CENTRAL IOWA...WILL CONTINUE TO OVERSPREAD THE 
STATE AS A WARM FRONT LIFTS NORTH.

HIGH PRESSURE WILL SLIDE ACROSS CENTRAL IA THIS 
EVENING WITH SOUTHERLY FLOW DEVELOPING AFTER MIDNIGHT AS THE HIGH 
SLIDES TO THE SOUTHEAST. WARM ADVECTION WILL THEN COMMENCE AND WITH 
THE SOUTHERLY FLOW AND INCREASING CLOUDS...TEMPERATURES WILL BE 
SLOWLY RISING TOWARD 6 AM.

HIGH PRESSURE WILL SLIDE ACROSS CENTRAL IA THIS 
EVENING WITH SOUTHERLY FLOW DEVELOPING AFTER MIDNIGHT AS THE HIGH 
SLIDES TO THE SOUTHEAST.

STRONG 
SURFACE GRADIENT WILL KEEP NW WINDS AT 20-28KTS ACROSS THE TAF 
SITES.
HAVE A GENERAL WARMING TREND INTO THE WEEKEND

STILL HAVE THE WEAK COLD FRONTAL 
BOUNDARY PUSHING THROUGH WEDNESDAY INTO WEDNESDAY NIGHT WITH MAINLY 
INCREASED CLOUD COVER DUE TO THE LACK OF MOISTURE.
WARM UP TO PEAK ON THURS

EXPECT ATMOSPHERE TO CONTINUE TO DECOUPLE...WITH WINDS DECREASING TO 
AROUND 15KT OVERNIGHT WITH OCCASIONAL GUSTS AS GRADIENT WILL STILL 
REMAIN TIGHT ACROSS THE AREA.

ANTICIPATE A WARMING TREND INTO 
THE WEEKEND PRIOR TO THE FIRST SHORTWAVE EJECTING FROM THE 
STRENGTHENING WESTERN TROF.

MVFR CEILINGS WILL 
LINGER NEAR DSM AND ALO THROUGH 01-02Z THEN CLEAR WHILE HANGING ON 
AT OTM UNTIL LATE THIS EVENING.

WITH WINDS STAYING UP MOST OF THE 
NIGHT AND TEMPS CONTINUING TO FALL BELOW ZERO

HOWEVER LOW CLOUDS ARE EXPECTED TO DEVELOP EITHER LATER THIS 
AFTERNOON OR OVERNIGHT WITH THE LOWEST CONDITIONS AFFECTING NRN 
SITES.

BUT COLD ADVECTION ALL DAY 
WILL RESULT IN FALLING TEMPERATURES THROUGH THE TEENS AND SINGLE 
DIGITS ON BREEZY NW WINDS.

THE MAIN SNOW THREAT THROUGH THE DAY TUESDAY SHOULD BE ACROSS 
THE SOUTHEAST HALF OF IOWA AND WILL INCLUDE A 3 HR WINDOW OF -SN AT 
KDSM/KOTM. -SN OR FZDZ POSSIBLE ELSEWHERE BUT CHCS DO NOT WARRANT 
INCLUSION IN TAFS ATTM. EXPECT CIGS TO LOWER THROUGH THE AFTERNOON 
WITH SOME MVFR FOG AS WELL.

I HAVE HYBRID TEMPERATURE CURVE THIS EVENING 
WITH TEMPS STEADY OR RISING A DEGREE OR TWO THEN FALLING AFTER 
MIDNIGHT.

INCREASED CLOUD COVER LATE 
TONIGHT...WITH LOW CLOUDS EXPECTED TO STAY MAINLY THROUGH SUNRISE 
THEN BEGIN TO EXIT FROM NORTHWEST TO SOUTHEAST THROUGH SATURDAY 
MORNING.

CONSIDERED A NON-DIURNAL TEMPERATURE TREND TODAY BUT SHOULD WARM UP 
ENOUGH LATER THIS MORNING INTO THE AFTERNOON ACROSS MUCH OF THE 
FORECAST AREA...SO HAD LOW CONFIDENCE IT WOULD BE WIDESPREAD ENOUGH 
TO MENTION.

NEXT SHORTWAVE LOOKS TO ENTER THE SOUTHERN PORTION OF THE STATE 
LATER THIS MORNING INTO THE AFTERNOON HOURS AND BRINGS ANOTHER
ROUND OF SHOWERS/TSTMS ACROSS THE FORECAST AREA INTO THIS
EVENING.

SHORTWAVE CURRENTLY OVER CENTRAL ALBERTA
WILL RACE QUICKLY SOUTHEAST PUSHING AN ARCTIC BOUNDARY THROUGH THE
STATE TONIGHT. RELATIVELY DEEP DENDRITIC GROWTH ZONE IN THE FAR
NORTHEAST AND WHILE LIFT IS NOT EXACTLY STRONG...IT WONT TAKE MUCH
TO PRODUCE SOME LIGHT SNOW IN OUR NORTHEAST THIS EVENING. FARTHER
WEST...SCATTERED SNOW SHOWERS ARE EXPECTED WITH SOUNDINGS
INDICATING A SHALLOW NEAR SURFACE MIXED LAYER DEVELOPING. THERE
MAY BE BRIEF PERIODS WHERE VISIBILITIES BECOME LOW WITH THE
FALLING SNOW AND STRONG WINDS BUT SUCH EVENTS SHOULD BE SHORT IN
DURATION. SOUNDINGS BEGIN TO DRY SUBSTANTIALLY AFTER MIDNIGHT WITH
PRECIPITATION ENDING LATE TONIGHT IN THE SOUTHEAST. HOWEVER...
STRONG COLD ADVECTION AND SUBSIDENCE ALONG WITH STRONG PRESSURE
RISES WILL LEAD TO DECENT NORTHWEST WINDS OVERNIGHT INTO TUESDAY
MORNING. SOME BLOWING SNOW IS EXPECTED IN FAVORED NORTHERN
LOCATIONS ALTHOUGH MUCH OF THE EXISTING SNOWPACK IS HARDENED BY
PREVIOUS WARM WEATHER WHICH MELTED AND THEN REFROZE THE SNOW. ANY
BLOWING SNOW WILL BE WHATEVER FALLS TODAY INTO THIS EVENING AND
WILL BE HELPED BY THE HARD NEARLY FRICTIONLESS EXISTING SNOWPACK.
IN ADDITION...WITH FALLING TEMPERATURES AND THE STRONG
WINDS...WIND CHILL VALUES WILL DROP INTO ADVISORY CRITERIA ACROSS
THE NORTH LATE TONIGHT INTO TUESDAY MORNING. THEREFORE...AN
ADVISORY HAS BEEN ISSUED FOR THESE AREAS.

MAIN CONCERN WAS CENTERED ON MVFR STRATUS DECK TO MOVE INTO THE
STATE THIS MORNING AND PERSIST INTO TUESDAY MORNING.

RIDGE OF HIGH PRESSURE WILL QUICKLY MOVE INTO IOWA THIS EVENING
BRINGING DRIER AIR AND LIGHTER WINDS TO THE STATE. THE RIDGE WILL
MOVE SWIFTLY AS WELL WITH A COLD FRONT ENTERING THE NORTHERN PLAINS.
THIS WILL BRING SOUTHWEST WINDS AND WARM ADVECTION BACK INTO THE
REGION WITH STEADY TO RISING TEMPERATURES AFTER MIDNIGHT. OVERNIGHT
LOWS WILL BE IN THE UPPER 20S FAR NORTH TO THE MID 30S
SOUTH...RISING TO THE MID TO UPPER 30S BY 6 AM. PARTLY TO MOSTLY
CLOUDY SKIES TO BEGIN THE EVENING THEN CLEARING AS SUBSIDENCE
ARRIVES.

PARTLY TO MOSTLY
CLOUDY SKIES TO BEGIN THE EVENING THEN CLEARING AS SUBSIDENCE
ARRIVES.

After lows in the mid 40s to mid 50s over the region this 
morning...the increasing weak warm air advection and gradual 
moistening of the mid layers in the next 24 hours will result in 
overnight lows about 8 to 10 degrees warmer at most locations with 
mins in the mid 50s east to the upper 50s central and west.

Winds have gradually become light south over the 
region today and this trend will continue tonight into Tuesday.

Temperatures 
for tonight should be a few degrees warmer than they were this 
morning...especially in western Iowa as WAA continues.

VFR conditions are expected to persist tonight. Clouds are
expected to increase on Monday.

Temperatures will be
much warmer tonight with cloudy skies and relatively moist low
levels allowing for minimal cooling.

Still anticipating MVFR to IFR ceilings to move into the state
overnight into Tuesday morning.

Mins tonight should be warmer than last night as H850 
temperatures will be roughly 4C warmer by 12z Friday morning than 
this morning across the region.

Models trying to develop some low
stratus or fog late tonight with low level moisture trapped
beneath the area of high pressure building in from the west.

Given the light winds late tonight and cold airmass in 
place, temperatures are forecast to drop below freezing for much of 
central Iowa.

MVFR ceilings will linger a few hours longer than previous 
forecast. Still, expect conditions to improve into VFR with gusty
winds become light overnight.

With overnight lows warming from 
yesterday into the lower 60s north to the mid 60s south; highs 
tomorrow will climb into the mid to possible upper 80s south and 
in the lower 80s north.

There is also a low chance of SHRA/TSRA at times overnight
and Monday, but confidence in location and timing, and expected
duration, are too low to include in the TAFs at this time.

Early morning highs in 
the mid to upper 30s northwest to the upper 40s south central to the 
mid 50s southeast...will give way to falling temperatures the 
remainder of the day.

Otherwise, the IFR ceilings look to
persist for much of the day with some gradual improvement this
afternoon before dissipating by this evening. Delayed the exit of
the stratus as models are slower to move it east and fairly high
confident to see the stratus linger into the early part of this
evening.

Lows tonight
will be about 5 degrees warmer west and central while the northeast
will finally see about a 10 degree warmer overnight low compared 
to last night.

High clouds
will move across the area overnight into Friday morning, however
they will not impact flight categories.

Lows tonight 
will be much warmer than previous nights with mins in the upper 
60s to low 70s.

Line of showers and storms looks to come through overnight. Enough
confidence to include VCTS at all TAF sites. Kept vsbys at 6 SM as
rainfall rates may not be too intense. Will, of course, monitor
and adjust as necessary.

Cooler, but pleasant conditions today will give way to increasingly 
colder, breezy, and stormy conditions this evening and overnight.

VFR will prevail through the daytime hours, giving way to MVFR 
overnight as TSRA/SHRA begin to blossom over the area. Eventually,
as TSRA/SHRA activity continues, ceilings will drop toward and 
into IFR conditions and sustain through the remainder of the TAF 
period. Additionally, winds will pick up this evening and 
overnight out of the N/NE around 15 kts, gusting to around 25 kts.

For most tonight will be much warmer than this 
morning.

VFR Ceilings were lowering across IA at 05z with light rain across
western sections. These trends will continue into the night with
MVFR conditions developing central and south by mid-morning as the
light rain persists in these areas.

With west-southwest winds starting near the 
adiabatic warming region, stronger WAA is expected on Saturday that 
will result in warmer temperatures across the forecast area for 
Saturday afternoon.

Ceilings will remain widespread through the forecast period
although some partial clearing is expected in southern Iowa. These
ceilings are expected to be VFR with visibilities remaining
unrestricted for the forecast period. Surface winds are expected
to remain south tonight and become light and variable on Saturday.

In fact, 
temperatures overnight have increased by a couple degrees already 
and will continue to warm through the morning.

Cigs will
lower overnight but still some uncertainty how low cigs will
become with any stratus as there remains a lack of any MVFR or
lower cigs in the vicinity outside of southeast TX. Have
maintained a MVFR forecast for most sites though with moisture
lifting north. Increasing southeast wind overnight will become
w/nw with fropa on Thu.

Mild 
westerly downslope flow is occurring behind the trough and that will 
allow temperatures to slowly rise for much of the overnight before a 
shift to more northwesterly winds occur late.

Thereafter, ceilings improve to VFR with southwest winds becoming
northwest by Saturday morning. Much of Saturday can expected VFR
conditions with west to northwest winds.

Colder temps and blustery winds follow 
the system tonight, which will drop wind chills into the single 
digits and teens below zero by Sunday morning.

Hires models do generate 
some isolated to scattered light precip along a surging cold front
to the south of the sfc low, but sufficient saturation is a 
struggle and the near surface fgen never matures. Just some low 
PoPs will suffice for now.

Temperatures will continue to rise early this morning with southerly 
flow.

Otherwise, wind shift tomorrow from S to W to NW will occur 
through the late morning and afternoon hours across the area.

Otherwise, strong SW flow will push temperatures 25+ degrees 
warmer than yesterday and have used a blended NBM 75th/BCConsshort 
to continue pushing temps over baseline NBM with the tendency for 
guidance to fall short in these situations.

LLWS will
begin the TAF period with strong near surface winds lingering into
the early to mid morning hours before easing. Similarly gusty SW
winds overnight will continue into the morning and ease from NW to
SE through the morning and afternoon. Gusts up to 35+ kts may be
seen at times, especially SE around KOTM as mixing increases
and before pressure gradient eases during the afternoon.

As such, temperatures may only drop a few degrees this 
evening before gradually warming through the overnight.

VFR conditions expected to continue through the TAF period. Main
concern continues to be LLWS later this evening into the early
overnight hours. Winds out of the south tonight become out of the
west to northwest tomorrow morning before returning to
south/southeasterly by tomorrow early evening.

These clouds should exit leading to plenty
of sun today, and with temps already warming tonight, highs 
should reach the 50s or lower 60s behind the passage of our 
downslope warm front.

Confidence is high in VFR conditions and little in the way of
clouds today.

Cloud cover is expected to stream in this evening ahead of the 
approaching system which will help keep low temperatures slightly 
warmer than this morning, but temperatures will still be below 
freezing across the north half or so of the area.

Clouds should
continue to lower and thicken but remain VFR until at least
midday. Precipitation is also expected to develop during the
morning, with rain or snow possible.

Another 
quiet night is expected with light winds and cool temperatures but 
slightly warmer than last night as warm advection begins early 
Monday morning along with an increase in cloud cover around 
daybreak.

Winds will shift
from northerly to southeasterly tomorrow.

Overnight temperatures tonight will
be warmer compared to the last few nights due to increased clouds
and subtle WAA entering the region.

Moisture continues to move into Iowa overnight, which will
continue to develop stratiform cloud cover across Iowa. For the
first few hours, ceilings will remain VFR.

With cloud cover 
increasing, temperatures will remain a bit warmer than last night, 
generally in the 50s.

As the high pressure takes hold
this afternoon, winds are expected to calm down becoming 
generally light and variable, as has been observed across parts of
northwest into central Iowa, before increasing slightly and 
becoming out of the east to southeast tonight.

Persistent warm air advection from the strong southerlies will keep 
low temperatures slightly warmer tonight.

Winds out of the southwest will
remain gusty through the overnight hours and into much of 
tomorrow with low level wind shear beginning after sunset and 
impacting all sites except KOTM.

Low temperatures tonight will 
also be warmer than the last few nights and in the low to mid 60s.

Minimal changes are expected into tonight with clear skies and light 
winds continuing through the evening hours before clouds start to 
move in late tonight into tomorrow morning as a boundary sets up 
oriented roughly northwest to southeast through the state.

The cloud cover and wind shift will help keep 
temperatures tonight a few degrees warmer than last night, but 
still in the mid 40s to low 50s.

VFR conditions will prevail overnight. Light showers will then
move in on Friday morning, persisting for several hours before
moving out/tapering off later in the day.

Temperatures tonight will be 
a few degrees warmer, generally in the 40s to low 50s, but highs 
will remain similar through the rest of the weekend, in the low to
mid 70s.

VFR conditions forecast through the period with SCT/BKN high
clouds AOA 10 kft and southeast wind.
-Warmer temperatures today into Thursday.

Non-convective low level wind shear will continue to affect the
terminals this morning with strong low level flow just off the
surface.

Shifting winds turning southwesterly are also expected 
ahead of this system, which is expected to increase temperatures 
through the night into Friday morning allowing for a non-diurnal 
trend into the 20s and 30s, warmest south.

Main concern will be the light snow band tracking over the area
through 14z. The main area is still back near FSD at 0535z and
should make it to ALO by 11-13z. Expecting IFR cigs and very
possible 1/2sm vsby as the band passes through MCW/ALO. Lesser
impacts expected at FOD,DSM and OTM for snow. Winds pick up aft
15z and some potential during the snow and aft 15z of BLSN;
especially MCW and potentially FOD and ALO. Later in period aft
18z a slight improvement in cigs prior to approaching Sat
snow. /rev

Therefore, temperatures may drop slightly into the 
evening but the anticipation is for a leveling then slowly rising 
overnight as strong warm advection persists.

VFR conditions are expected to prevail across all TAF sites
through the period. The only items of concern may be some LLWS
overnight, and some gusty southerly winds creeping into KOTM and
possibly KDSM by during the day Saturday.

Temperatures 
will only continue to rise from here with low temperatures having 
occurred earlier this evening around 03Z.

VFR conditions expected through the TAF period. Main aviation 
concerns are LLWS here this morning at mainly KALO/KDSM/KOTM and 
breezy winds out of the southwest gusting up to around 30 knots
during the daylight hours and primarily affecting southern sites.
Breezy winds are expected to decrease by around sunset.

Conditions will also remain warmer tonight into tomorrow morning 
with low temperatures tonight about 10 degrees warmer than they were 
this morning.

Winds will become southeasterly after sunrise and 
become gusty in the afternoon for southern terminals.

Temperatures do still drop into the 40s, a few sites 
potentially still seeing some upper 30s where more efficient 
radiational cooling occurs, but this is still warmer than this 
morning!  

The omega block in place today, with upper level ridging extending 
border to border north to south in the central US between the former 
Great Lakes low continuing to move towards the eastern US coast and 
another low just off shore of California, does still break down 
through the day Thursday as the western low treks onshore.

VFR conditions prevail through the period. Winds will be light 
with variable directions tonight. However, the predominant flow 
will be out of the southwest to south through tonight and 
tomorrow.

Tonight will be warmer and more humid as 
southwest flow returns and H850 temps warm to the upper teens to 20C 
by 12z Tuesday.

Storms expected
to dissipate after sunset with winds becoming southerly for the
remainder of the period.

Mins tonight will begin the ramp up process with a 10 
to 15 degree warmer overnight low most areas with mid 60s east to 
the upper 60s west.

Confidence is high in continuing VFR conditions with nothing more
than spotty high cloudiness through at least tomorrow morning. 
Winds are not expected to decouple much with persistent +/- 10kt 
sustained winds into the morning, and minor gusts into daytime 
mixing Saturday. This pattern will also result in a period of LLWS
west and north early Saturday morning.

As the low 
shifts across the upper midwest overnight cloud cover will increase 
across northern to central Iowa, helping to keep temperatures a few 
degrees warmer than last night, in the upper 20s.

Little change is anticipated through the period with high
confidence in VFR conditions continuing and nothing beyond 
occasional mid and high level cloudiness. No appreciable wind 
changes are expected.

Today will see highs early this morning 
with slowly falling temperatures the remainder of the afternoon into 
the evening.

Several concerns including ongoing winds/gusts, snow chances and
lower visibility due to blowing snow and falling snow this
afternoon. Sites along and west of I35 (FOD,MCW,DSM) still taking
the brunt of wind today into evening while slightly lesser wind
expected at OTM, ALO. Needless to say, but very poor conditions
will continue through period. /rev

As alluded to 
over the last several forecast cycles, this non-diurnal temperature 
trend with warming temperatures through the overnight will allow us 
to move out of wind chill headlines sooner in the west/south into 
portions of central Iowa and have adjusted headlines accordingly so 
much of the area will see the Wind Chill Advisory expire at 9Z/3AM 
with the exception of east central/northeast areas which continue 
until 14Z/8am.

VFR conditions are expected to persist through 18z. There will be
increasing chances for light snow across parts of the area during
the afternoon and evening. There remains some question on moisture
available that will impact both snow chances and cig levels but
potential is there for MVFR cigs. Will add further details as
confidence increases. Breezy west wind early will gradually
diminish during the period.

Lows tonight will drop to the single digits northwest to 
the mid teens in the south.

Some mixing evident today when sun has appeared, but still
looking at lingering MVFR southeast near OTM through 19-20z and
small risk DSM may see brief period between 21-00z.

Southwest surface flow will work to boost temperatures 
further with highs in the southern half of the state in the mid 
40s.

VFR conditions to prevail through the period. Winds to decrease
in speed through the day and lose gusts by 21z.

With clearing 
overnight, lows will drop to the lower 20s in the northwest to the 
mid to upper 20s in the southeast.

IFR and MVFR cigs to continue to move off to the east over the
next 6 hours, taking with it lingering rain and snow. Winds will
remain elevated tonight with 20kt gusts possible, especially in
the east.

Lows will drop to the lower to mid teens
north while central to southern areas drop to the upper teens 
to near 20.

Stratus continues over the region with breezy winds. Mainly VFR
conditions with a few pockets of MVFR cigs. Flurries continue to
form through afternoon, though limited in coverage. Winds will
continue gusting to 30kts; especially north. Tonight the cigs
will thin somewhat with winds relaxing to near 12kts.

With colder air advecting into the area, clearing skies, and 
diminishing winds, expecting some efficient cooling through the 
night with temperatures dropping into the low to mid 30s by early 
Friday morning.

Breezy daytime winds
from the northwest will relax tonight becoming from the west.

Temperatures are forecast to remain warmer than last night 
with increasing moisture and clouds helping to curtail radiational 
cooling despite light winds.

Confidence is high that VFR conditions will persist through much
of the period with high cloud ceilings well into Friday, and
possibly some smoke aloft as well.

Overnight will be similar to last night with 
clear skies, light winds and temperatures slightly warmer than this 
mornings.

Overnight will be similar to last night with 
clear skies, light winds

Once skies clear and 
winds diminish, temperatures should plummet with the favored cold 
areas likely dropping below freezing.

MVFR conditions expected to give way to VFR for most of the
period aft 02z. Models are suggesting potential for some brief
3-5sm BR near FOD around 12z. Otherwise winds become light/var
aft 04z and then shift southeast/south toward 18z and generally
under 12kts through 00z. /rev

Meanwhile, 
with extensive clouds tonight and Wednesday, lows overnight will be 
somewhat milder than last night and dropping to the lower 20s north 
to the lower 30s in the south.

Winds out of the southeast will shift through
the night settling out of the northeast into Wednesday morning,
but generally staying near to below 10 knots.

The warmer 
start to the day will unfortunately not last very long, especially 
in northern Iowa, where the second stronger cold front will reach 
first but later this morning into midday before sinking south 
through the rest of the area through the afternoon hours. As a 
result, high temperatures will also be earlier in the day than 
typical peak heating for most. Although still advertised in the low 
to mid 30s north and low 40s south, as we have been saying for the 
last several days, it won't feel like much of a warm-up today with 
the winds having already started to increase with gusts to 20 mph 
having already been noted in some locations across central Iowa. 

This is just the start of our winds today which will become 
exceptionally gusty through the day, the strongest winds/gusts this 
afternoon into mid evening, especially in the north to northeast. 
Have expanded the Wind Advisory through the entire area for a number 
of reasons. 1) We continue to see all the signals that lead to 
strong wind days from strong cold air advection, an increasing 
pressure gradient, steepening lapse rates, strong subsidence, and 
strong surface pressure rises, which notably all maximize near to 
behind the front in the main time frame noted of this afternoon into 
mid-evening. 2) Gusts in North Dakota early this morning near to 
just behind the front have peaked over 50 knots (57 mph) already 
with a better wind parameter space coming together this afternoon 
closer to Iowa (and surrounding region). 3) Soundings continue to 
suggest winds at the bottom of the mixed layer around 35 to 39 knots 
(40-45 mph), which based on everything we've seen looks to be the 
low end of our wind potential today. At the top of the mixed layer, 
winds peak closer to 40 to 50 knots (45-55+ mph) and given the 
parameter space, we are likely to reach some of these higher gusts. 
So, as noted, Wind Advisory will be in effect across the area from 
just before midday to 6Z/midnight tonight with winds staying gusty 
well into the evening before diminishing gradually overnight, though 
remaining quite gusty through the night, just below advisory 
criteria. The timing of the headline is a little fast in the south 
but kept it simple with the main message that it will become quite 
windy today with sustained winds of around 25 to 35 mph and gusts of 
45 to 55 mph, the highest gusts north central to northeast Iowa. 
Also cannot rule out some gusts over 55 mph, but will let next shift 
continue to evaluate trends should an upgraded headline be 
needed in portions of northern/northeastern Iowa. Be sure to 
secure any outdoor holiday decorations now!

Besides the wind and falling temperatures which will notably become 
quite cold by tonight with lows in the single digits for most of the 
area and low teens in the south, the elevated winds through the 
night will cause feel-like temperatures to bottom out below zero 
with single digits below zero in the south to near 15 or more below 
zero in the north.

Winds from the southwest will become from the northwest through
the morning hours and increase in speed. Wind gusts have been 
increased to at least 40 knots at the northern sites of MCW, 
FOD, and ALO. It remains possible that a few wind gusts around 
50 knots may occur in the afternoon hours over northern Iowa.
Accompanying the increasing winds will be lowering ceilings 
into MVFR that will teeter around FL020 and may for a short time
drop below this FL. Have now included a short period of MVFR 
stratus at DSM where confidence is above 50% in occurrence.

Temperatures will steadily fall into 
tonight with clouds departing by sunrise most areas. Overnight 
mins will drop to the upper teens northwest and to the mid 20s 
southeast.

MVFR ceilings are the common restriction across central Iowa
early this evening, but improvement into VFR is expected 
through the evening from west to east. Did slow that improvement
into VFR at ALO and OTM by a few hours from previous issuance.
Otherwise, breezy winds from the northwest will prevail
overnight into Sunday morning before decreasing in the afternoon
and becoming from the southwest toward the end of the period.

The low pressure system currently centered 
over southern Iowa will continue to track northeastward into the
Upper Midwest today, which will gradually bring cooler 
temperatures for all areas of the state later today.

Surface winds remain strong from the
northwest this afternoon and this evening but slowly weaken 
into Monday morning.
- 'Cooler' today with highs in the 80s in most central Iowa towns

IFR and MVFR ceilings are common at terminals north of I-80 
this morning as low stratus settles into the state. However,
this stratus will begin to move to the northeast and to scatter
later this morning with VFR conditions returning by early 
afternoon at all official forecast sites. The timing of this was
slightly delayed in this issuance to account for the latest 
trends in guidance. VFR conditions will prevail as winds from 
the northwest become light and variable late this afternoon and 
evening with winds becoming from the southeast by the end of the
period.

With no significant change to the airmass overhead, our hot and 
humid temperatures will continue again today, albeit slightly cooler 
than yesterday with slightly cooler 850 mb temperatures overhead. 
Highs are expected to climb into the upper 80s north to low 90s 
south, with heat indices around 100F for much of the area.

However, there is also a low chance 
for an isolated storm as early as this afternoon, and this could
impact any site. Confidence in location/timing/occurrence is 
too low to include in any TAF, but will keep an eye on trends 
and update accordingly.

Temperatures continued to slide this afternoon and will continue to 
do so as winds ease this evening. Lows tonight will bottom out into 
the negative teens for much of the area.

Mostly VFR conditions are expected during the period. Some
localized MVFR/IFR cloud streamers associated with the cold air
this afternoon should dissipate this evening. Breezy northwest
wind will also diminish and become light and variable at times.

Between these, strong low level warm air 
advection will set up and bring milder air into Iowa.

However, cloud 
cover will be stout, especially over northern into central Iowa

Temperatures have been warming through the night and will 
continue to warm today with highs near to below freezing over 
snowpack and in the 30s over the less-snowy southwest.

Partly cloudy skies and light
winds prevail through the afternoon and evening,

However, temperatures are expected 
to drop back below freezing again tonight and may lead to a re-
freeze of any liquid that's collected from the melting snow. Be 
cautious of slick spots on roadways and sidewalks as 
temperatures drop off tonight.

Fog development is possible again tonight, but with too many
competing factors, have left out of TAFs at this time.

Temperatures will continue to decrease this evening and especially 
overnight as clouds depart and winds remain breezy out of the 
northwest, with overnight lows expected to fall into the single 
digits north and in the teens south.

Strong and gusty northwest winds will persist into the mid
evening then will gradually diminish the remainder of the night.

Southwest winds aloft 
have already started today, some of that flow translating to the 
surface near the MO River. This means that temperatures will warm 
overnight for the south/west.

VFR conditions are expected to prevail during this cycle. A
frontal passage will move thru the terminals between 10-14z.
This may lead to a brief period of lower VFR CIGs, but any 
precipitation is expected to remain north and east of 
terminals. LLWS has been maintained in all terminals overnight, 
as a strong 50+ knot SWLY LLJ develops atop of sfc southeasterly
winds. Sfc winds will shift out of the northwest behind the

Expect winds to gust up around 30 KT through mid
to late afternoon before abating by early this evening.

High mvfr cigs extend from rfd to ord and should be

In addition, by Tuesday night, a strong cold front is forecast to

Rain showers will increase in coverage by this evening with the
area under a favored channel for long duration waves of showers
through Tuesday. Visibility and ceilings will likely show
fluctuation given the showery nature, but in general IFR 
conditions are favored. Thunderstorms are likely in the region 
tonight into Tuesday, looking slightly more favored from mid- 
evening through the overnight.

As the new surface low rapidly lifts northward to northern lower
Michigan by 12z Monday and deepens to the high 980s mb, strong
cold advection will result in steadily falling temperatures.

Periods of rain are expected to continue through 12-13Z with 
occasional "breaks" with light rain/drizzle in between the more 
moderate rain showers and occasional higher ceilings.

Another cool September night is in store again today, albeit 
warmer than last night, which should limit our frost potential for
most areas.

There are no major weather concerns through the period. Expect 
VFR flying conditions, with only some high level clouds/smoke on 
Sunday. Winds are expected to remain southeasterly through the 
period.

Overnight temperatures will stay warmer than they have been the past 
few nights thanks to persistent southwest flow with lows in the 
lower to mid 40s areawide.

Modest southwest winds and
generally clear skies can be expected across the area prior to the
front arriving. A 30-35 kt low level jet will spread across the
area prior to sunrise, with some sporadic gusts of 15-20 kt
possible at times at the surface.

850 mb temperatures do not vary much over the next 24 hours. Given 
the amount of cloud cover that will remain over the region, I expect 
Monday morning lows to be warmer than this morning, but Monday highs 
will barely reach into the 70s, while southern locations may stay in 
the upper 60s.

Subtle surface high pressure ridge was noted across southern WI
and northern IL late this afternoon, while a warm front stretched
from KS into central MO and far southern IL. This warm front is
expected to move slowly north into central IL through Monday, in
response to a mid-level disturbance which will lift slowly
northeast into the area. Modest warm/moist ascent associated with
this disturbance was already producing rainfall across parts of
IA, MO and west-central IL, and the northern edge of this
precipitation shield will lift east-northeast toward the terminals
into Monday morning. High-res computer models are in general
agreement in keeping the bulk of the more moderate precip south of
the terminals, roughly south of the Interstate 80 corridor.
However, lighter showers along the northern periphery of this area
of rain will be close if not into especially the southern-most
Chicago metro terminals during the day. Based on this scenario,
have maintained mention of prevailing low-impact (no vis
restriction) showers across KGYY and KMDW, with a prob30 mention
a bit farther north at KORD and KDPA. KRFD will likely remain dry
even farther north. High-res guidance is also in good agreement
with developing and expanding MVFR ceilings into the Chicago metro
terminals as well Monday afternoon and evening, though this will
be most likely where some rainfall occurs and moistens lower
levels. Uncertainty therefore exists, with the potential for some
deviation in placement seen in current model depictions.

Overnight lows will be just a bit warmer than this 
morning's lows.

It is another repeat performance this evening as southerly winds
with some SSW component slacken off a bit and trend more SSE.

With little change in the atmosphere 
under the ridge, low temperatures Sunday morning will be just 
slightly warmer than this morning's low temperatures, mainly in the 
mid to upper 60s.

VFR conditions with SW/WSW around 10 knots are expected for the 
Chicago metro terminals through at least early Sunday afternoon.

An upper level trough over the Mississippi River valley remains 
cutoff from faster and more zonal flow over much of southern 
Canada. At the surface, high pressure centered over New England 
extends westward across the local area and will keep quiet weather
in place tonight. Winds will drop off once again allowing for 
decent cooling, though overnight lows should be a couple degrees 
warmer than last night.

All is quiet on the aviation front tonight with high pressure in
control. The light wind speeds overnight into Tuesday morning may
become variable in direction at times.

Our cool spell continues in the short term, although temperatures
tonight should end up a few degrees "warmer" than they were this
morning thanks to an anticipated thickening stratus deck with
time.

Winds tonight will be very light thanks to an expansive area of 
surface high pressure persisting over the region with calm 
conditions already observed in some places this evening. The mid- 
level clouds from this afternoon continue to erode. Occasional 
cirrus will pass through overnight with another area of mid-level 
clouds expected to move in by Thursday morning. There is a non- 
zero chance for a few flurries/sprinkles in the morning, but have
maintained a dry TAF with this issuance. Winds trend more 
southwesterly during the day tomorrow remaining under 10 kt.

Wind gusts will ease this evening, but warm air advection will
continue off the surface as a ~35 kt southwesterly low-level jet 
sets up tonight ahead of the upper level impulse shifting 
eastward across the Upper Midwest. This should thus keep 
overnight lows tonight a bit warmer than the past few nights, with
readings expected to be generally in the 30s.

Pleasant flying weather continues into the weekend as the area
remains on the western edge of a surface high. A cirrus cloud deck
is currently advancing towards the area from eastern Iowa which
will move across our terminals overnight. Some high VFR ceilings
are possible at RFD and surrounding areas as the clouds pass
through.

Thursday will start off cool and sunny, but clouds will increase 
fairly quickly by late morning as a pool of seasonably cool 850mb 
temperatures of -10C or so spreads overhead atop the warming 
boundary layer. Accordingly, the diurnal rise in temperatures 
tomorrow will be muted with highs "only" topping off in the upper
30s.

VFR conditions are expected through the period amid gusty W 
winds. Gusts to 20 knots are expected through daybreak, then 
increase to around 30 knots late morning through the afternoon. 
The sustained speed to gust spread may be fairly large at times, 
with a couple sporadic gusts nearing 35 knots possible this 
afternoon even as sustained winds remain under 20 knots. Gusts 
will diminish to under 25 knots with nocturnal decoupling this 
evening.

Fairly quiet conditions are expected through this afternoon ahead
of a slow-moving low-level trough currently stretching from 
western Lake Superior into the central Great Plains. A band of mid
to upper- level clouds forced within the right-entrance of a 
120kt upper-jet streak will gradually shift south across the north
half of the CWA through the day. Otherwise, persistent SW winds 
gusting up to 25 mph will bring in milder conditions as temps rise
to near freezing.

Wind gusts late this evening over the area have started to
gradually ease, though still occasional gusts to 25 kt being
observed over/near the Chicago metro. As the winds inch their way
a little more southwesterly, the speeds will ease in through 
daybreak. As for the low-level jet overhead, this is being sampled
at 45-55 kt around 2,000 ft on area Doppler Radar Vertical Wind 
Profilers (VWPs) and AMDAR aircraft soundings. This should 
continue through about 08Z and then gradually ease. Profiles are 
favorable for low-level wind shear and so no change with that in 
the TAFs.

The main story through the daylight hours Wednesday will be the 
expected strong SSW winds beginning this evening and continuing 
through most of the day Wednesday. A 70kt LLJ will quickly develop
over northern Illinois this evening in tandem with a 
strengthening surface pressure gradient in advance of low pressure
taking shape over the central High Plains. While some diurnal 
stability will develop tonight, the magnitude of surface 
decoupling should be subdued by the cirrus shield and overall 
strength of the low-level flow. Expectations are for frequent 
S/SSW gusts around 30 mph late this evening through daybreak 
Wednesday. Meanwhile, the associated strong WAA (temps rising into
the 40s overnight) and moisture advection will act on eroding 
some of the remaining snow cover.

60 knot low-level winds will persist well into Wednesday as low- 
level moisture surges into the area. Meanwhile, stratus will 
quickly develop and expand over the CWA. This leads to lower 
confidence on the ability for full mixing into stronger winds 
aloft. However, with 50 knot winds down to 1.5kft mid-morning into
the afternoon, little mixing will be needed to attain frequent 
gusts over 40 mph. Held off on the issuance of a Wind Advisory for
the southeast half of the CWA, but some gusts to 45 mph (advisory
criteria) are possible.

With the increase in low-level moisture, WAA, and additional 
deep- layer ascent, showers should begin to increase in coverage 
across primarily the northwest half of the area late morning and 
especially in the afternoon. If the amount of low-level moisture 
increases more than expected, the stratus may lower enough that 
some pockets of drizzle develop.

A 65 to 70 knot LLJ will quickly develop late this evening and 
continue over the Chicago terminals through the night. Winds as
high as 60 to 65 knots may extend as low as 1.5kft during the 
strongest period overnight. At the surface, winds will veer SSW 
by late evening while increasing in conjunction with the LLJ. 
Surface gusts to 30 knots are expected through much of the night.

Temperatures will be milder overnight than last night, thanks to 
modest south winds and increasing boundary layer moisture. Lows 
will dip into the upper 50s along the IL Lake Michigan shore where
an onshore wind component has brought chillier marine air, but 
most of the area will see lows in the lower 60s.

The main focus of the going TAFs is the winds, which will be quite
breezy throughout much of the TAF period. Any residual gusts to
about 20 kts or so occurring late this afternoon should cease for
the most part as the sun begins to set, but sustained winds to 
around 10 kts out of the south will continue through the overnight
hours. Gustiness will pick up shortly after daybreak on Sunday and
will peak during the afternoon, where gusts in excess of 30 kts 
will become commonplace. These gusts may come down a bit and/or 
become less frequent as we head into the evening hours on Sunday, 
but at least intermittent gusts of 25-30 kts (possibly higher 
depending on how much deep mixing can be sustained after sunset) 
could still be seen through the end of the current 30-hour TAF 
period for ORD and MDW.

Mid and high level cloud cover will be on the increase later 
tonight in advance of the next approaching weather disturbance now
shifting over the Dakotas. This should help keep overnight low 
temperatures tonight warmer (in the upper 50s to around 60) than 
what was observed this morning.

Lake breeze will make it through ORD and MDW early this evening
before washing prior to reaching DPA. After a couple hours of  
east to northeast winds at start of TAF period, winds should go
light/variable or calm tonight.

Conditions tonight 
will be quiet and warmer than last night through most of the night,
with the main period of interest being just prior to dawn through
about mid morning Tuesday.

A ridge of high pressure will crest the area tonight which will
allow the current breezy northwest winds to become light and 
likely somewhat variable into the late evening and overnight 
hours. A southeasterly direction is favored Tuesday morning with a
more sustained south to southwest direction developing through 
the afternoon from west to east. The exception will be GYY which 
should remain easterly for much of the day thanks to the proximity
to the lake, but low level southerly wind speeds should be enough
to overcome the lake influence late in the afternoon.

A light south 
wind tonight will keep temperatures a few to several degrees 
warmer than last night.

Winds over the past several hours have been teetering on either side 
of southerly. This will likely continue through the remainder of the 
evening and through the night. However, gusts will cease near or 
prior to 02Z and sustained wind speeds will subside to near or under 
5 kts shortly thereafter. Such conditions will persist through the 
overnight before winds establish a SSW direction and pick up to just 
under 10 kts by mid-morning on Saturday.

Lows tonight should be a smidge "warmer" than
last night, but still expecting a smattering of mid 30s in our
typical cool spots, particularly across parts of the Fox River
Valley.

Overall quiet conditions are expected through the TAF period with 
high pressure still in place across the region. Winds become light 
and variable overnight then returning to a prevailing east and then 
northeast direction Friday (mainly under 10 kt) reinforced by a 
weak lake breeze during the afternoon. CIGS remain VFR with a few
3000 ft strato- cumulus clouds possible during the day.

Southerly flow has enveloped the area and will continue through
the next couple days as broad but strong low pressure develops and
consolidates across the Northern Plains. This return flow is
largely dry tonight, although residual stratus across far eastern
Illinois and central/southern Indiana is expected to be pulled 
northward over at least northwest Indiana this evening. This 
stratus is thin (500-1000 ft) per diagnostic soundings, but 
trapped under a strengthening inversion, so is should hold its 
own as it gets shoved north. Also passing high clouds elsewhere 
will lead to a variable nature of sky cover. Enough of a clear sky 
in north central Illinois initially this evening may offset the 
southerly winds for a few degree temperature drop, but after that 
the entire CWA should experience a slow temperature climb.

There is an area of MVFR stratus (~1500ft) that is surging NNE at
this hour along the IL/IN stateline, soon to reach GYY and MDW. 
It is becoming more probable that this reaches ORD and possibly even
DPA. For now have SCT015 mention there, but a short-fused AMD for
MVFR cigs may be needed. Timing the back edge of the stratus
generally expect this to lift northeast of the area sometime 
between 6-9Z returning cigs to VFR.

Temperatures are now slowly rising and will continue to rise into
this afternoon. Highs today and on Sunday are likely to reach the
lower to mid 40s south of I-80, but there remains uncertainty for
highs over the deeper snow pack across northern IL and have 
capped highs both days in the mid 30s. Across the Chicago metro, 
upper 30s to near 40 seem possible.

Southerly winds are already showing sporadic gusts early this
morning and those should become prevalent by mid-morning. Also in
that time, the direction is expected to veer from 160-180 degrees
at daybreak to 190-210 by 15Z. While there is some snow cover to
keep from mixing to a maximum potential depth today, gusts should
still reach the mid 20 kt range easily with sporadic higher.

However, we are 
expecting a quick recovery in temperatures on Sunday thanks to a 
return to breezy south winds and increased sunshine. While some 
gustiness up to 35 mph is likely during the day, high temperatures
should top out well into the 50s to the low 60s during the 
afternoon.

As a surface ridge continues to moves overhead this evening, 
expect skies to clear and winds to go light and variable.

Gusts of up to 
20-25 knots will persist through tonight as NE winds today veer 
ENE with a secondary wind shift mid-evening. NE winds to 15 knots 
will then continue during the day Thursday.

Lows tonight should be
warmer than last night especially with increasing cloud cover
later tonight, generally upper 50s/lower 60s.

Disturbance will move across the region Tuesday which could be
enough to overcome the dry air and allow for some scattered
showers to develop during the morning into the early afternoon.
Rain chances appear to be a bit higher with westward extent, so
added a PROB30 in for RFD. Later TAFs may need to introduce some
light rain chances farther east into the Chicago terminals. 

Otherwise, generally light winds expected through early Thursday
morning. Lake breeze should cause winds to flip more northeasterly
Tuesday afternoon at ORD, MDW, and GYY.

Heading into Monday, deep mixing is anticipated which will help 
temperatures warm back into the lower 70s. Dewpoints will also 
respond by dropping into the 30s, with some guidance suggesting it
could be even lower. This combined with winds gusting into the 
20-25mph range would create increased fire spread risk, especially
given the anticipated lower precip amounts today.
Any lingering showers move out Sunday evening.

Persistent south-southwest 
flow and associated warm advection will also boost our 
temperatures well into the 70s across much of the area, and we may
tag 80 in a few spots across far northern IL where increasing 
afternoon cloud cover ahead of the aforementioned wave will be 
last to develop.

Prevailing southwesterly winds stay breezy at the surface. A 
strong low level jet with winds over 40 knots at 925 mb is 
resulting in LLWS through Tuesday morning. With sufficient mixing,
a occasional stronger gusts at the surface are possible, but 
confidence was too low to add it to the TAF at this time.

Winds are then forecast to increase once again late Tuesday
morning with stronger gusts around 25 knots Tuesday afternoon
remaining out of the southwest. As the sun sets and the 
restrengthening of the low level jet, it looks like winds will 
once again stay breezy at the surface with LLWS aloft.

Lows should
be a bit milder than this morning thanks to the higher dewpoints
that are advecting.

Winds this evening will likely remain under 10 kts, and may even
go light and variable at times.

This 
will continue to foster northerly (northeasterly at ORD and MDW) 
winds at the terminals this afternoon before speeds ease and 
directions back more west-northwesterly tonight.

While this will make for a rather chilly start to the day 
on Tuesday, warm air advection is expected to kick up on Tuesday 
following the quick eastward progression of the surface ridge 
axis. A return to southerly winds during the day should help 
temperatures rebound back into the lower to middle 30s under some 
increasing high-level cloudiness during the afternoon.

The gusty NW winds will be stepping down through this evening and 
should be steady at under 10 kt by around 06Z or shortly thereafter.

A band of upper-level clouds at press time will clear the area by 
daybreak allowing for a sunny start to the day. With temperatures 
running some 10 degrees warmer this morning compared to yesterday 
morning, high temperatures today will be similarly 10 degrees warmer 
and in the low to mid 40s.

Winds will
generally be light and just west of south; however, given the
variability, brief periods of light winds east of south are
possible through 15Z. Winds will trend to become more east of
south after 18Z before becoming more easterly later in the
afternoon. There is still a little uncertainty in the exact
timing, but there is moderate confidence that by 21Z, light winds
will be more south of east and remaining through the end of the
TAF period.

Expectation is that this drizzle will 
taper off a little later this morning as the stratus deck 
gradually becomes more shallow and less favorable for producing 
precipitation beneath the synoptic dry slot. Otherwise, skies will
remain cloudy through the day with breezy southwest winds 
gradually diminishing. Between the cloud cover and persistent low-
level cold advection, temperatures will likely only rebound a few 
degrees from our morning lows. Still, temps near 40/lower 40s 
remain above-average for late December.

Expectation is that this drizzle will 
taper off a little later this morning as the stratus deck 
gradually becomes more shallow and less favorable for producing 
precipitation beneath the synoptic dry slot. Otherwise, skies will
remain cloudy through the day with breezy southwest winds 
gradually diminishing.

On a positive note, the gusty winds tonight into Sunday will 
set up a good warm-advective pattern across the region.
Accordingly, progressively warmer temperatures are expected over
the next few days. For Sunday, readings are expected to top out 
in the upper 30s in the snow covered areas south of I-80, and 
into the low to mid 40s in the snow free areas of northern IL.

Only forecast concern this period remains the winds. Southwest
winds will continue to gust into the lower 30kt range through
the early overnight hours and slowly diminish into the mid 20kt
range during the predawn hours, as directions turn more
westerly. Winds will likely turn a bit more west/northwest mid/
late Sunday morning with gusts continuing into the lower 20kt
range. Speeds/gusts will diminish Sunday afternoon and to less
than 10kts with sunset Sunday evening.

Expect the snow to gradually abate for most areas from northwest 
to southeast later this evening into the overnight.

The snow then cold from Friday night and Saturday will soon be
vanquished from our memories as we leap right back into spring 
the next few days. While there will be some passing mid-high level
cloudiness from time to time today, there should be plenty of 
sunshine mixed in to support high temps climbing into the upper 
50s to mid 60s. This is on the higher end of the spectrum for high
temps today, since every mild day we're seen the past few weeks 
has had temps peak near the top of the guidance spectrum.

South-southwesterly surface winds will increase into the 10-15 
kt range overnight, in association with an area of low pressure 
passing well north of the forecast area. A fairly strong low- 
level inversion will likely prevent much in the way of surface 
wind gusts until after sunrise, though above the inversion a 
southwesterly low level jet will increase to 40-45 kts during 
the pre-dawn hours and will present LLWS conditions. As low 
level mixing deepens after sunrise and ends the LLWS threat, 
surface winds will become gusty as they being to tap into the 
bottom of the low level jet. Some gusts 20+ kts are possible 
early, though should ease by mid-morning and will continue to 
diminish Sunday afternoon. A dissipating cold front will slip 
into the area Sunday evening shifting winds more light westerly,
likely becoming light and variable after midnight.

Dry and seasonably cool conditions today will give way to 
increasing temps and gusty southwest winds for Monday. The 
combination of dry conditions, clear skies tonight, and nearby 
surface ridge will support another night with good radiational 
cooling. Moderation of the airmass over the past day will yield 
somewhat warmer conditions than last night, with lows generally
in the mid 30s to locally low 30s away from the core of the 
Chicago metro.

Breezy west-northwest winds ease with sunset this evening 
becoming light out of the west southwest around 5kt through the
rest of the overnight hours. The lake breeze is expected to 
remain east of ORD/MDW though it may still get close enough to 
MDW for the direction to become somewhat variable after sunset 
(under 5kt) before returning to a westerly direction shortly
thereafter.

In the wake of elevated fire weather conditions this afternoon,
breezy southwesterly and much milder conditions are in store 
tonight, in the warm sector of the fast moving clipper-like 
low pressure system that will affect the region through 
tomorrow night. A thickening cloud deck along with the 
southwesterly winds gusting up to 25-35 mph will keep low temps 
propped up in the lower to mid 50s.

Scattered showers will continue to move across the terminals
over the next few hours. There may be a brief vis reduction in
the heaviest showers, but otherwise vfr cigs/vis expected and
these will end by 08z-09z.

After any lingering overnight convection clears the area this
morning, the already breezy southerly winds will get even 
breezier by mid-morning as we begin to tap into 40 kt flow in 
the lower part of an overhead low-level jet. This will likely 
translate to 40-45 mph gusts being observed during a brief window
of time between the mid-morning and early afternoon before the 
magnitude of the gusts lessens a bit as the low-level jet 
continues to gradually wane going into this afternoon. These 
southerly/south-southwesterly winds will also serve to advect in
an unseasonably warm and moist air mass, characterized by 
summer-like dew points in the low to mid 60s and temperatures 
that will likely climb into the upper 70s to around 80F with the
assistance of some filtered sunshine.

Height rises, large-scale subsidence on the backside of the 
departing upper-level trough, and the development of a capping 
inversion should ensure that most of our forecast area will remain 
dry through the daytime hours. However, by about the mid-afternoon, 
the capping inversion will likely be eroded as a result of surface 
heating, and some combination of broad isentropic ascent and low-
level confluence should help isolated to scattered convection to 
sprout. Confidence is highest in this occurring in our southern 
counties, where high resolution models continue to suggest that 
there may be a zone of more focused ascent, but can't entirely rule
out a stray shower/storm or two popping up elsewhere, so continue
to carry slight chance PoPs across the entire CWA during the 
mid-late afternoon. There will be a plentiful amount of instability
around come this afternoon (MLCAPE of up to around 2500 J/kg), so
would not be surprised if a couple of storms managed to grow deep
enough to support a threat for downbursts and/or hail, but the 
latest thinking is that the relatively broad and modest forcing 
for ascent should preclude the development of any overly 
rambunctious convection capable of making full use of the available
instability.

Meanwhile, to our west and southwest, a frontal zone is expected to 
light up with convection during the afternoon and evening as large 
scale forcing for ascent increases in advance of another upper-level 
trough ejecting into the Great Plains. Convection that originates in 
Iowa and Missouri is likely to grow upscale with time and track in 
our general direction, with most of the latest CAM runs envisioning 
that at least a semi-organized multicell storm cluster will be 
knocking on the doorstep of our western CWA by mid-evening. While
these storms are expected to lose steam with time and eastward 
extent, forecast soundings indicate that the degree of available
buoyancy here this evening could still be adequate to support the
development of new, deep updrafts along the storm cluster that 
would carry a threat to produce strong to severe downburst winds,
particularly across our northwestern CWA. This threat largely 
hinges upon this storm cluster developing a robust consolidated
cold pool that would be able to overcome increasing nocturnal 
boundary layer stability, which does not appear to be a given at
this time.

Of additional interest with tonight's thunderstorms is the potential 
for localized flash flooding. It does not have the look of an ideal 
flash flood setup by any means, but it does appear that storm 
orientation could somewhat align with storm motion vectors for a
time and promote some potential for training convection. The 
nose of a strong low-level jet to our southwest will also pivot 
in our direction tonight and provide a continuous replenishment 
of moisture into the region, which will likely keep thunderstorms
and heavy rainfall ongoing in at least part of our forecast 
area throughout the night. Thus, some potential for localized 
minor flooding does seem to exist in our forecast area tonight, 
and WPC's Marginal Risk in their Day 1 Excessive Rainfall 
Outlook continues to look appropriate for highlighting this 
possibility.

Shower and storm coverage is likely to diminish after daybreak on 
Sunday as the low-level jet diurnally weakens. However, with surface 
low pressure and an associated cold front still to our west, warm 
conveyor belt showers and storms will likely continue in some 
capacity in our forecast area during the day on Sunday, with 
the highest chances for precipitation remaining across our 
western counties through sunset.

On May 14, 2024, the Biden administration announced a comprehensive increase in tariffs on approximately $18 billion worth of Chinese imports, targeting strategic sectors like electric vehicles, semiconductors, and solar cells. [3, 6] While the new duties included some critical minerals, the administration deliberately excluded others where China holds significant global market control, such as germanium, gallium, and rare earths. [8] This selective approach was designed to avoid disrupting supply chains for materials where the U.S. has a high dependency on China, highlighting a strategic decision to apply pressure without creating immediate domestic shortages. [8]

On July 6, 2023, the Pentagon confirmed it maintains a strategic stockpile of germanium, a crucial material for high-speed computer chips and military applications like night-vision devices. [1] A spokesperson stated that while there is a reserve for germanium, there is currently no inventory for gallium. [3] In response to supply chain vulnerabilities, the Department of Defense is proactively using its authority under the Defense Production Act to increase the domestic mining and processing of critical materials, including both germanium and gallium, to support the microelectronics and space supply chains. [1, 3]

On July 3, 2023, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and General Administration of Customs announced new export controls for germanium, gallium, and related chemical compounds, which became effective on August 1, 2023. [2, 4, 7] These measures, intended to protect China's national security and interests, require Chinese exporters to obtain specific licenses before shipping these materials. [5, 7] The implementation of these controls was expected to disrupt global supply chains and potentially increase prices for numerous products, particularly in the semiconductor, solar panel, and electric vehicle industries. [2, 7] The United States, which classifies both metals as critical to its economic and national security, was significantly impacted by these regulations throughout the remainder of the year, including the fourth quarter of 2023. [2, 7]

Morgan Stanley forecast that Chinese lithium carbonate prices would fall from approximately $67,500 per metric ton in the first half of 2023 to $47,500 per metric ton in the second half of 2023, projecting a decline driven by easing EV battery demand and growing supply.

<1> In a report published on May 29, 2022, Goldman Sachs declared the bull market for battery metals, particularly lithium, was "over for now." The investment bank forecasted a significant drop in lithium prices, citing a surge in supply that would outpace demand growth. Goldman Sachs projected that after averaging around $54,000 a tonne in 2022, lithium prices would plummet to $16,372 a tonne in 2023. The report explained that a rush of investor capital into supply-side projects created a "fundamental mispricing" and an outsized supply response ahead of the actual demand trend. The release of this bearish forecast prompted a significant sell-off in lithium stocks.

<2> In a research note published on November 30, 2023, Goldman Sachs analysts projected a significant global lithium surplus for 2024, estimating it to reach 202,000 tonnes. [4] This forecasted surplus, which represents 17% of the anticipated global demand, is expected to place continued downward pressure on lithium prices throughout the year. [4] The investment bank's bearish outlook is attributed to a substantial increase in supply, particularly from new and expanding projects in Australia, China, and Chile, which is set to outpace the growth in demand from the electric vehicle and energy storage sectors. [4, 8] This oversupply has contributed to a sharp correction in lithium prices from their previous highs. [1, 4]

<1> Following an 80% price collapse in 2023, lithium carbonate prices experienced a modest 10% recovery to US$14,859 per tonne in early 2024, as reported by Motley Fool on April 3, 2024. However, this analysis suggested the price increase was not a fundamental market shift. This view is supported by financial institutions like Goldman Sachs, which predicts that a market bottom for lithium prices will not be reached until 2025 due to ongoing imbalances between supply and demand.

<1> On February 8, 2024, Goldman Sachs released a forecast, maintaining a bearish outlook on the lithium market due to anticipated oversupply. The investment bank predicted that lithium prices would not bottom out until 2025. The forecast estimated average 2024 prices for lithium carbonate at $13,377 per tonne and lithium hydroxide at $14,263 per tonne. Other reports from Goldman Sachs around the same period featured slightly different but comparable price forecasts, consistently pointing to a market bottom in 2025 before a potential recovery in 2026.

On March 20, 2025, President Trump signed an executive order titled "Immediate Measures to Increase American Mineral Production." This directive is part of a broader initiative to enhance the domestic production of critical minerals, such as lithium, and lessen U.S. dependence on foreign suppliers. The order mandates several key actions, including expediting the permitting processes for mining projects, prioritizing mineral extraction as a primary use for relevant federal lands, and delegating authority to the Secretary of Defense to use Defense Production Act (DPA) funds for strategic domestic resource projects.

In the fourth quarter of 2024, U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods, including lithium-ion batteries, led to an estimated 15% increase in import costs. This development significantly impacted the automotive sector and was projected to potentially slow the growth of the electric vehicle (EV) market by 10%. Concurrently, the tariffs served as an incentive for domestic lithium production, encouraging investments in U.S.-based extraction and processing ventures.

<4> During the third quarter of 2025, investor sentiment in the lithium market was negatively impacted by uncertainty surrounding US policy. This stemmed from the Trump administration's plans to roll back electric vehicle (EV) tax credits and a perceived retreat from the Inflation Reduction Act, which rattled investors. The federal EV tax credit, which provided up to $7,500 per vehicle, was officially terminated on September 30, 2025, following the passage of the 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' in July 2025. The announcement of the credit's termination led to a surge in EV sales in August and September as consumers rushed to make purchases before the deadline. Despite this short-term sales boost, the medium-term outlook for the lithium market turned more bearish due to the policy changes. The period was also marked by significant price volatility in the global lithium market.

text: A market analysis of the U.S. lumber industry for January 2023 revealed a stronger-than-anticipated start to the year, with performance more aligned with pre-pandemic norms. [1] Following nine consecutive weekly price drops at the end of 2022, the market showed relative stability. [1] The Random Lengths Framing Lumber Composite Price (FLCP) experienced a minor decrease of $17 for the month, marking the sixth consecutive monthly drop but also the smallest monthly change since March 2020. [1]

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: Improved weather conditions towards the end of March 2023 spurred an increase in lumber demand, which allowed sawmills to extend their order files and increase prices. For the week ending March 24, 2023, the price of Western Spruce-Pine-Fir 2x4s rose by $16, reaching a new price of $380 per thousand board feet.

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: For the week ending April 19, 2024, the Madison's Lumber Prices Index fell by 8% to US$444 per thousand board feet (mfbm). This represented a significant decrease of $37 from the previous week's index of US$481 mfbm. The decline in lumber prices was linked to buyer hesitation following a substantial drop in US single-family housing starts for March, which was reported as the largest decrease since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic in April 2020.

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: In April 2024, the Producer Price Index (PPI) for softwood lumber saw a significant seasonally adjusted increase of 6.2% from the previous month, marking the largest month-over-month rise since January 2022. This contributed to a 0.5% increase in overall construction input prices for the month. Annually, overall construction input prices were up 2.3% compared to April 2023. The broader PPI for final demand rose 0.5% in April, with the yearly increase at 2.2%.

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: <1> In early 2024, analysts predicted a modest increase in lumber prices, influenced by anticipated growth in single-family housing starts and sustained demand for repair and remodeling. Projections from the National Association of Home Builders on February 27, 2024, forecasted a 4.7% increase in single-family starts for the year, reaching an annual rate of 988,000 units, with a further 4.2% rise expected in 2025. This expansion in home building was expected to create supply-side challenges, leading to higher prices for lumber, lots, and labor. At the start of the year, lumber prices were indeed in the mid-$400s per thousand board feet. For example, the RoMac Building Supply Wood Commodity Index stood at $464.13 in January 2024. Another index reported a price of $474 per thousand board feet for the week ending January 19, 2024.

text: For the week ending July 12, 2024, the Madison's Lumber Prices Index stood at US$369 per thousand board feet (mfbm). [1, 2] This represents a 3% decrease, or $11, from the previous week's index of US$380 mfbm. [2]

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: On August 8, 2024, the forest products industry price guide, Madison’s Lumber Reporter, published a market update for the week ending July 26, 2024. target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: Lumber prices saw a notable increase in mid-October 2024, with the benchmark Western Spruce-Pine-Fir 2x4 lumber reaching US$402 per thousand board feet for the week ending October 18, 2024. [1, 2] This marked a 4% increase, up $14 from the previous week's price of $388. [1, 2] An October 18 report confirmed that while prices had somewhat stabilized compared to previous years, the market remained sensitive to changes in supply and demand. [5] The price strength was underpinned by supply-side restrictions, as numerous mill curtailments and closures across the U.S. and Canada helped to limit inventory. [3, 5, 8] Following this period, reports in early November indicated that the upward price trend for framing lumber had continued throughout October. [4, 8]

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: In the first week of March 2025, the U.S. lumber market was thrown into turmoil by a rapid series of trade policy announcements. On March 4, 2025, the Trump administration imposed a 25% tariff on most goods entering the U.S. from Canada and Mexico. [6] This move, which was in addition to existing duties on Canadian softwood lumber, created significant uncertainty for buyers and sellers, threatening to disrupt supply chains and increase costs for homebuilders. [3, 6] Just two days later, on March 6, the administration reversed course, announcing a one-month delay until April 2 for tariffs on products from Canada and Mexico that are covered by the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). [2, 6] The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) worked with the White House to ensure Canadian lumber was included in this temporary pause. [3, 6] This abrupt imposition and subsequent delay of tariffs caused considerable confusion within the industry. [6]

target_variable: lumber USD 1000 board feet [Commodity market price]
text: <2> In April 2025, the North American lumber industry confronted significant challenges, including ongoing permanent mill closures, the threat of escalating tariffs, and potential supply constraints, all while consumer demand remained below pandemic-era peaks. [10] The industry has seen a substantial reduction in capacity, with about 5 billion board feet permanently taken offline. [10] Specific closures around this period included International Paper's Campti, LA facility on April 11, 2025, and San Group's plants in British Columbia. [8] The tariff situation was a major point of uncertainty; a proposed 25% tariff on Canadian goods was ultimately exempted for softwood lumber on April 2, avoiding a sharp increase. [2, 5] However, the industry still faced existing duties of around 14.5% and the prospect of these rates rising later in the year. [2, 11] These factors, combined with timber shortages from environmental issues and other supply chain disruptions, contributed to projections of moderate price increases through the spring. [1] [7] The market softness was attributed to a post-pandemic recalibration in demand, which was approximately 9% below its recent highs, and sluggish new home construction. [10]

text: <1> Russ Taylor Global has forecasted that US domestic lumber prices will experience a sharp increase by the second quarter of 2026. This anticipated price spike is driven by tightening supply and shortages resulting from ongoing U.S. trade restrictions and tariffs on Canadian lumber exports, which will fail to meet seasonal rises in domestic demand.

US Magnesium, the only primary producer of magnesium in the United States, notified the Utah Department of Workforce Services in September 2024 that it would be laying off 186 employees and idling its plant operations in Skull Valley. [3, 4, 8] The layoffs were scheduled to take effect on or around November 25, 2024. [3, 7] The company attributed the decision to a 90% drop in lithium carbonate prices since 2022. [6, 8] While this was the official reason, lithium production constitutes a small portion of the company's overall operations at its Great Salt Lake facility. [3, 4] US Magnesium expressed hope that the layoffs and suspension of operations would be temporary, contingent on the recovery of lithium carbonate prices. [4, 6, 8] The company is also facing a lawsuit from a contractor for allegedly unpaid invoices totaling nearly $5.8 million. [6, 8]

On February 24, 2023, the American Iron and Steel Institute (AISI) reported that based on preliminary Census Bureau data, the U.S. imported 2.61 million net tons of steel in January 2023. [1] This figure represented a 14.4% decrease compared to the same period in January 2022. [1, 2] As steel production is the primary consumer of manganese, a significant change in steel import volumes can influence domestic steel production and, in turn, affect the demand for manganese.

In its August 2023 mineral industry survey, the U.S. Geological Survey reported that U.S. imports of manganese ore experienced a significant decline to 475 metric tons, a sharp drop from 42,100 metric tons in July 2023. [3] The survey also noted that average spot prices for manganese ore delivered to China were 3% lower than in July 2023 and 23% lower than in August 2022. [3] Coinciding with these market changes, a military coup occurred in Gabon on August 30, 2023. [3, 5] Gabon is the world's second-largest producer of manganese. [3, 5] Following the coup, the leading manganese producer in the country, Eramet Group, temporarily suspended its operations on August 30 but resumed production the next day. [3]

Data released by the World Steel Association on April 21, 2023, showed that U.S. crude steel production totaled 6.7 million tonnes in March 2023, a 2.1% decrease compared to March 2022. [1, 5] For the first quarter of 2023, U.S. steel production was 19.4 million tonnes, representing a 4.0% decrease from the same period in 2022. This downward trend in steel production, a key manganese-consuming sector, offers a direct indication of manganese demand.
